events.text:
Got an offer today. Here's the CTC annexure they sent, pasted as it came:

    Basic                            12,00,000
    House rent allowance              6,00,000
    Special allowance                 4,50,000
    Employer PF                       1,44,000
    Gratuity                            57,720
    Performance bonus                 3,00,000
    Joining bonus                     2,00,000
    Group medical premium               24,000
    Total CTC                        29,75,720

Starting 1 June 2026. What am I actually getting? I want the monthly number.

Before anything is computed, here is what I have read off your annexure. Correct
anything that is wrong — nothing runs until you say it is right.

| Line, as your letter names it | Amount | Period | Type | From |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | 12,00,000 | annual | `basic` | "Basic 12,00,000" |
| House rent allowance | 6,00,000 | annual | `hra` | "House rent allowance 6,00,000" |
| Special allowance | 4,50,000 | annual | `special_allowance` | "Special allowance 4,50,000" |
| Employer PF | 1,44,000 | annual | `employer_pf` | "Employer PF 1,44,000" |
| Gratuity | 57,720 | annual | `gratuity` | "Gratuity 57,720" |
| Performance bonus | 3,00,000 | annual | `variable_pay` | "Performance bonus 3,00,000" |
| Joining bonus | 2,00,000 | annual | `joining_bonus` | "Joining bonus 2,00,000" |
| Group medical premium | 24,000 | annual | `insurance_premium` | "Group medical premium 24,000" |

Financial year 2026-27, from the 1 June 2026 start date.

Two things I did not find in what you pasted, and both change the reading if
they exist elsewhere in the letter:

- **Any condition attached to a line** — a recovery period on the joining bonus,
  a tenure condition, a "subject to" clause. The annexure carries none. If the
  offer letter's body does, quote it to me.
- **Any equity** — no grant appears here. If there is one in the letter, it needs
  its own questions before it can be read at all.

Is the table right?
Yes, that's right. No clawback on the joining bonus, and there's no equity.

basis.rationale: The base component of the salary structure, payable monthly under the terms of employment whatever the employee or the employer achieves.
Paid with monthly salary as part of the fixed structure. Its exemption from tax is conditional on rent paid; the payment itself is not.
The residual monthly allowance that balances a structure to its agreed fixed pay, and is paid unconditionally like the rest of it.

document.title: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (No. 19 of 1952)
The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (No. 39 of 1972)

basis.rationale: Quoted at a target and paid against an assessment of performance, so neither its occurrence nor its amount is settled by the letter. It is offered each year, and it is cash in the year it is paid.
Promised unconditionally for joining, paid in cash, and paid once.
A premium the employer pays to an insurer every year. The employee receives cover, and never the money.

citation.section: The Code on Wages, 2019 (No. 29 of 2019), section 2(y)(i)

document.title: The Code on Wages, 2019 (No. 29 of 2019)

citation.note: Section 2(y) defines wages and lists what they include: "(i) basic pay; (ii) dearness allowance; and (iii) retaining allowance, if any". Basic pay is the first of the three and is its own head, distinct from the other two. Of this file's catalogue entries only `basic` is basic pay; a dearness or retaining allowance entry added to the catalogue is a different head of wages and does not belong here, even though the two share a base with basic pay under the provident fund and gratuity Acts.

citation.section: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, sections 2(b) and 6

document.title: The Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (No. 19 of 1952)

citation.note: Section 6 computes the contribution on "basic wages, dearness allowance and retaining allowance", and section 2(b)(ii) excludes house rent allowance from basic wages by name, along with overtime, bonus and commission. Of the catalogue's entries only `basic` is inside that base; this file carries no dearness or retaining allowance entry yet, and a ticket adding one must add it here too. Whether a "special allowance" falls inside section 2(b) has been litigated and is not settled by the section's own words, so it is left out rather than guessed at.

rate_citation.section: The paragraph beginning "Under the EPF, Scheme, 1952, an employee of any covered establishment"

document.title: Ministry of Labour and Employment, reply to Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 586, 24 July 2023 (PIB release 1942083)

rate_citation.note: Read this before quoting the figure, and read `employee_rate`'s note with it: the same caveat applies for the same reason. Section 6 says "The contribution which shall be paid by the employer to the Fund shall be ten percent. Of the basic wages, dearness allowance and retaining allowance, if any", and its first proviso substitutes "12 percent" for notified establishments "at both the places where they occur" -- that notification could not be retrieved. So 0.12 is the rate the Government states is applied, not the rate read off the section: "The employer is also required to contribute 12% of the wages." This is the WHOLE employer share. Section 6A(2)(a) diverts part of it to the Employees' Pension Scheme, but the Act fixes only a ceiling on that part -- "not exceeding eight and one-third per cent of the basic wages, dearness allowance and retaining allowance" -- and leaves the figure itself to "as may be specified in the Pension Scheme", which could not be retrieved. The split is therefore not carried here, and a figure computed from this rate is the employer's total contribution rather than what reaches the provident fund alone.

citation.section: The paragraph beginning "The wage ceiling for coverage under the EPF Scheme, 1952"

document.title: Ministry of Labour and Employment, reply to Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 586, 24 July 2023 (PIB release 1942083)

citation.note: Read this before quoting the figure. "The wage ceiling for coverage under the EPF Scheme, 1952 is revised from time to time. Presently, it is Rs.15000/- per month since 01.09.2014." Section 6 of the Act carries no ceiling at all -- it lives in the Employees' Provident Fund Scheme, 1952, whose consolidated text could not be retrieved, and the 2014 notification that set it could not be retrieved either. This is the Government's statement of the figure, not the instrument that fixed it.

citation.section: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, section 2(s)

document.title: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (No. 39 of 1972)

citation.note: '"wages" means all emoluments which are earned by an employee while on duty or on leave in accordance with the terms and conditions of his employment and which are paid or are payable to him in cash and includes dearness allowance but does not include any bonus, commission, house rent allowance, overtime wages and any other allowance.' Of this file's catalogue entries only `basic` is inside that base -- house rent allowance is excluded by name, and a special allowance by the closing words -- and a dearness allowance entry added to the catalogue must be added here too.

citation.section: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, section 4(2) and its Explanation

document.title: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (No. 39 of 1972)

citation.note: "For every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months, the employer shall pay gratuity to an employee at the rate of fifteen days' wages based on the rate of wages last drawn by the employee concerned." The Explanation fixes the divisor: "In the case of a monthly rated employee, the fifteen days' wages shall be calculated by dividing the monthly rate of wages last drawn by him by twenty-six and multiplying the quotient by fifteen." Two provisos to the same sub-section put a piece-rated and a seasonal employee outside this formula, and neither is encoded here.

citation.section: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, section 4(1)

document.title: The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (No. 39 of 1972)

citation.note: "Gratuity shall be payable to an employee on the termination of his employment after he has rendered continuous service for not less than five years" -- on superannuation, on retirement or resignation, or on death or disablement. The first proviso waives the five years where the termination is due to death or disablement, so the period bounds a resignation and not every ending of the employment.

citation.section: Income-tax Act, 2025, Schedule III (see section 11), Table Sl. No. 11 ("Any special allowance from employer"), read with section 202(2)(a)(i)

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: Read this before saying anything about HRA. Schedule III excludes from total income "any special allowance from employer" where "such allowance is specifically granted to meet expenditure actually incurred on payment of rent (by whatever name called) in respect of residential accommodation occupied by the assessee", the accommodation "is not owned by him", and he "has actually incurred expenditure on payment of rent". HOW MUCH is exempt is not in the Act. Condition (b) of the same entry reads "such allowance is to such extent as may be prescribed having regard to the area or place in which such accommodation is situated and other relevant considerations", so the limbs of the exemption -- and the definition of "salary" that decides whether basic bounds it -- live in the rules prescribed under the Act, not in the Act. No primary text of those rules could be retrieved: incometaxindia.gov.in refuses requests from this environment. This file therefore states that the exemption exists and is bounded by a prescribed extent, and does not state the bound; a figure for it cannot be computed from this file. Section 202(2)(a)(i) excludes Schedule III Table Sl. No. 11 from the computation of total income by name, so the exemption is the old regime's alone.

events.text:
Run one is done, and it raises one question I would rather confirm than ask
cold.

Your letter states an employer PF contribution of **₹12,000 a month, ₹1,44,000 a
year**. That is not a policy statement, but the policy is inside it. At the 12%
employer rate the two possible wage bases give:

- **the whole of basic** — a wage of ₹12,00,000, so a contribution of
  **₹1,44,000**;
- **the ₹15,000-a-month statutory ceiling** — a wage of ₹1,80,000, so a
  contribution of ₹21,600.

Your letter's figure lands exactly on the first. So your employer looks to
compute provident fund on the whole of basic rather than capping at the ceiling.

**Is that right?** If your payslip or HR says otherwise, say so and I will use
what you tell me — this is a reading of your letter, not an answer about your
employer.

One optional extra while you are here: if you know the **annual professional
tax** your state levies, tell me the figure and I will put it in the deductions.
Without it, professional tax is named among the things the estimate leaves out.
Yes — full basic. I don't know the professional tax figure offhand.

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: "75000 or the salary, whichever is less, where income-tax is computed under section 202(1)" -- so it is capped at the salary it is deducted from. Section 202(2)(a) disallows only Sl. No. 1 of the same table, which is the tax on employment, so the standard deduction survives in the new regime.

citation.section: Income-tax Act, 2025, section 516 ("Rounding off of amount of total income, or amount payable or refundable")

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: "rounded off to the nearest multiple of 10 ignoring any part of a rupee consisting of paise and thereafter if such amount is not a multiple of ten" -- increased if the last figure is five or more, reduced if it is less than five. Dropping the paise first and rounding the whole-rupee figure on its last digit gives the same answer as rounding the exact amount half upward, because the paise can only decide the outcome at an exact rupee ending in five, where both readings round up.

citation.section: Income-tax Act, 2025, section 202(1) Table ("New tax regime for individuals, Hindu undivided family and others")

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: Charged for tax year 2026-27 by the Finance Act, 2026, section 3(1), which refers to these rates rather than restating them. Finance Act, 2026, section 56 is its only amendment to section 202 and touches sub-section (2)(a)(iii) alone, leaving this table untouched. The Act states the table as band and rate without spelling out the marginal arithmetic; it is read as a slab table, which is how the Income Tax Department's own calculation engine applies it.

citation.section: Income-tax Act, 2025, section 156(2) and (3) ("Rebate of income-tax in case of certain individuals")

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: Available to a resident individual only. Section 156(2)(b) also gives marginal relief where total income exceeds twelve lakh rupees, which this decoder does not yet compute, so the figures above the threshold are the pre-relief ones.

citation.section: Finance Act, 2026 (No. 4 of 2026), section 3(15) ("Health and Education Cess on income-tax")

document.title: The Finance Act, 2026 (No. 4 of 2026)

citation.note: Charged on the income-tax as increased by the applicable surcharge, and so on the tax remaining after any rebate. Imposed by the annual Finance Act rather than by the Income-tax Act: it must be re-sourced each year.

citation.section: Income-tax Act, 2025, section 516 ("Rounding off of amount of total income, or amount payable or refundable")

document.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (No. 30 of 2025)

citation.note: The same section and the same unit: "any amount payable or refundable under this Act" rounds to the nearest ten rupees. The 1961 Act's section 288B rounded tax to the nearest rupee; the 2025 Act carries no such provision, and a search of its full text finds no other rounding rule outside the tonnage-tax chapter.

events.text:
Here is the decode, with the monthly figure at the end of it.

## What is guaranteed, recurring and cash

- **Guaranteed recurring cash: ₹22,50,000** — Basic, House rent allowance and
  Special allowance.
- **Headline CTC: ₹29,75,720** — every line above, Basic through Group medical
  premium.

Those are the two figures to hold side by side. Five lines of the letter are in
the second and not the first, each for a reason carried on the line itself:

| Line | Amount | Why it is not guaranteed recurring cash |
|---|---|---|
| Employer PF | ₹1,44,000 | guaranteed, recurring, but `locked-savings` — it goes into the fund, not to you |
| Gratuity | ₹57,720 | `conditional-on-tenure` and `deferred-cash` |
| Performance bonus | ₹3,00,000 | cash and recurring, but `conditional-on-performance` |
| Joining bonus | ₹2,00,000 | guaranteed cash, and not recurring — it arrives once |
| Group medical premium | ₹24,000 | guaranteed and recurring, but a `benefit-in-kind` |

Grouped as the decoder totals them:

- **Variable pay at target: ₹3,00,000** — Performance bonus.
- **Retirals: ₹2,01,720** — Employer PF and Gratuity.
- **One-time: ₹2,00,000** — Joining bonus. No clawback period is attached to it.
- **Benefits in kind: ₹24,000** — Group medical premium.
- **Fixed pay: ₹26,75,720** — everything except the Performance bonus.

No component carries equity, so there is nothing to value and no equity figure
in this reading.

## Year by year

Four years, on two bases. Counting **no variable pay**:

- Year one is **₹24,50,000**; the average across the four years, with the
  one-time line in it, is **₹23,00,000**.
- Year 1 ₹24,50,000 = ₹22,50,000 guaranteed recurring cash + ₹0 variable +
  ₹2,00,000 one-time + ₹0 equity.
- Years 2, 3 and 4 are **₹22,50,000** each: ₹22,50,000 + ₹0 + ₹0 + ₹0.
- That average of ₹23,00,000 holds the Joining bonus, which arrives once. The
  same average without it is **₹22,50,000**.

Counting **variable pay at its quoted target**:

- Year one is **₹27,50,000**; the four-year average with the one-time line is
  **₹26,00,000**, and without it **₹25,50,000**.
- Year 1 ₹27,50,000 = ₹22,50,000 + ₹3,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 + ₹0; years 2 to 4 are
  **₹25,50,000** each = ₹22,50,000 + ₹3,00,000 + ₹0 + ₹0.

These totals are **not** the headline CTC. Retirals and benefits in kind sit
outside this table on purpose: they arrive on the same terms every year, so they
say nothing about what separates one year from the next. They are in the totals
above.

## Basic, and what it drives

Basic is **₹12,00,000**, which is **44.84%** of fixed pay of **₹26,75,720**.
The numerator is the Basic line alone; the denominator is Basic, House rent
allowance, Special allowance, Employer PF, Gratuity, Joining bonus and Group
medical premium.

Three rules compute on that figure:

- **Employer provident fund** — computed on the Basic line at **12%**, with a
  statutory monthly wage ceiling of **₹15,000**. Read the rate's own caveat: the
  Act's section 6 says *ten* per cent, and 12% applies to establishments the
  Central Government has notified; that notification could not be retrieved, so
  the 12% here is the Ministry of Labour and Employment's statement of the rate
  applied, not the rate read off the section.
- **Gratuity** — accrues on the Basic line at 15 days of wages per completed
  year, the monthly wage divided by 26, payable after 5 years of continuous
  service (Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, section 4(2) and its Explanation). No
  gratuity figure is computed anywhere in this reading.
- **House rent allowance exemption** — the Income-tax Act, 2025 settles that the
  exemption exists and leaves its extent "to such extent as may be prescribed".
  The rules file does not carry those limbs, so the exemption is bounded and the
  bound is not computable here.

## The employer's provident fund contribution

You confirmed the whole of basic, and that is what the take-home below uses. It
agrees with the letter: ₹1,44,000 is 12% of the ₹12,00,000 wage, where the
₹15,000-a-month ceiling would have given ₹21,600 on a wage of ₹1,80,000.

## Take-home

Two regimes, as two facts about the same letter. Which one applies to you is
not something this decides.

### Under the new regime

True only if: the new regime, a resident individual, and steady state — no
one-time component. The Joining bonus is therefore outside every figure below.

**Counting no variable pay**, on recurring cash of **₹22,50,000** a year,
**₹1,87,500** a month (Basic, House rent allowance, Special allowance):

- Employee provident fund **₹1,44,000** a year, **₹12,000** a month — 12% on the
  full basic wage of ₹12,00,000.
- Income tax: salary ₹22,50,000, less the standard deduction of ₹75,000, gives
  total income ₹21,75,000; tax at the slabs ₹2,43,750; no rebate; cess at 4% is
  ₹9,750; **tax payable ₹2,53,500**.
- Total deductions **₹3,97,500** a year, **₹33,125** a month.
- **Take-home ₹18,52,500 a year — ₹1,54,375 a month.**

**Counting variable pay at target**, on recurring cash of **₹25,50,000** a year,
**₹2,12,500** a month (the three above plus the Performance bonus):

- Same employee provident fund, ₹1,44,000 a year.
- Income tax: salary ₹25,50,000, less ₹75,000, total income ₹24,75,000; slabs
  ₹3,22,500; no rebate; cess ₹12,900; **tax payable ₹3,35,400**.
- Total deductions **₹4,79,400** a year, **₹39,950** a month.
- **Take-home ₹20,70,600 a year — ₹1,72,550 a month.**

### Under the old regime

True only if: the old regime, below 60 years of age, a resident individual, and
the same steady state.

**Counting no variable pay**, on the same ₹22,50,000 a year:

- Employee provident fund ₹1,44,000 a year — unchanged; it does not depend on
  regime.
- Income tax: salary ₹22,50,000, less the standard deduction of ₹50,000, total
  income ₹22,00,000; slabs ₹4,72,500; no rebate; cess ₹18,900; **tax payable
  ₹4,91,400**.
- Total deductions **₹6,35,400** a year, **₹52,950** a month.
- **Take-home ₹16,14,600 a year — ₹1,34,550 a month.**

**Counting variable pay at target**, on ₹25,50,000 a year:

- Income tax: total income ₹25,00,000 after the ₹50,000 standard deduction;
  slabs ₹5,62,500; cess ₹22,500; **tax payable ₹5,85,000**.
- Total deductions **₹7,29,000** a year, **₹60,750** a month.
- **Take-home ₹18,21,000 a year — ₹1,51,750 a month.**

### What these figures leave out

The same five under both regimes: HRA exemption, Chapter VI-A deductions,
employer NPS deduction, professional tax (you did not have the figure), and
perquisite tax on vesting equity. The first four would lower the tax; the last
would raise what is actually withheld in a year equity vests, and you have no
equity here.

Under the old regime the output adds one more line, and it is the one that
matters for reading the two side by side: excluding HRA exemption and Chapter
VI-A deductions **can only lower the old-regime figure further, never raise it**.
So the old-regime take-home above is a floor. The new-regime figure is not a
floor in the same way — the deductions it excludes are largely ones that regime
does not allow. The two numbers are not like for like, and there is no crossing
point in this output for me to give you.

## Flags

None. Nothing in this package crossed a threshold in `heuristics.yaml` and no
line carries a clawback or a cliff — which is a finding about the thresholds and
this letter, not a verdict on the offer.

- The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (No. 39 of 1972) — https://www.labour.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/06/072a4b7ea8246533c62b96b68a30da53.pdf
